props.title: International House
props.initialSlug: Comedy chaos erupts at Chinese hotel auction

sections.content: International House stands as a fascinating Pre-Code comedy that captures the anarchic spirit of early 1930s entertainment. The film's setting in a Chinese hotel becomes a perfect excuse to string together outrageous vaudeville acts and musical numbers, featuring an incredible lineup of talent including W.C. Fields at his sardonic best, Burns and Allen's rapid-fire wit, and Cab Calloway's electrifying "Reefer Man" performance. Like other Pre-Code films such as Baby Face (1933) and Design for Living (1933), it pushes boundaries with risqué jokes and sexual innuendos that would become impossible after the Production Code's strict enforcement in 1934.

sections.content: The film's structure - using a new invention demonstration as a plot device to showcase various performers - influenced later variety-style films like The Big Broadcast of 1938 (1938) and Star Spangled Rhythm (1942). The loose narrative framework allows for maximum entertainment value, throwing together blackout sketches, musical numbers, and comic routines in rapid succession. This variety show format would later evolve into the classic Hollywood musical revue seen in films like Thank Your Lucky Stars (1943). SUBHEAD: Pre-Code Freedom and Technical Innovation

What makes International House particularly noteworthy is its blend of technological prophecy (the "radioscope" invention) with uninhibited Pre-Code humor. Like Employees' Entrance (1933) and Red-Headed Woman (1932), it represents the brief window of creative freedom before censorship clamped down. The film's casual references to drugs, sex, and its generally risqué tone provide a fascinating glimpse into American entertainment before the Production Code's strict enforcement changed Hollywood's landscape.
